nameStory: The harpoon clubtail gets its name from the distinctive shape of its tail appendages, which resemble the pointed tip of a fishing harpoon. Like all clubtails, it also has that characteristic 'club' - a wider segment at the end of its abdomen that looks like someone attached a tiny paddle to the dragonfly's rear end.
description: The harpoon clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the clubtail family, known for their enlarged tail segments that look like little clubs. These dragonflies have the typical clubtail build with bright green eyes that are widely separated (not touching like many other dragonflies), a brownish-black body with yellow markings, and clear wings. Adults typically measure about 2-3 inches long with a wingspan around 3-4 inches. They're strong fliers that often perch on rocks, logs, or bare ground along waterways.

idTips.label: Clubbed abdomen
idTips.description: The tail end widens noticeably into a club-like shape, especially obvious when viewed from above - it looks like the dragonfly is carrying a tiny wooden club at its rear end

idTips.label: Separated green eyes
idTips.description: Bright green or blue-green eyes that never touch each other on top of the head, unlike many other dragonflies where the eyes meet in the middle

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often lands on bare ground, rocks, or logs with wings held perpendicular to the body, rather than hovering constantly like many dragonflies

idTips.label: Yellow and black pattern
idTips.description: Dark brownish-black body decorated with bright yellow stripes and spots, creating a bold contrast that's easy to spot against natural backgrounds

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with dark veining, no colored patches or bands - they make a crisp rustling sound when the dragonfly takes off

habitat: Look for harpoon clubtails along clean streams, rivers, and sometimes pond edges throughout New England, especially in areas with rocky or sandy bottoms. They prefer moving water with good oxygen levels and often hunt from perches on exposed rocks, fallen logs, or bare patches of ground near the water's edge. You'll typically find them in partially shaded areas where forest meets water.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. Larvae (nymphs) are developing in the muddy or sandy bottoms of streams and rivers, looking like small, drab, flattened insects.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for adult harpoon clubtails! Look for them perched along waterways from June through August, especially on warm sunny days when they're actively hunting and mating.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by early September. Mated females lay eggs in shallow water, and the dragonflies disappear as cooler weather sets in.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs and young larvae survive the winter, buried in stream sediments. No adults are visible during this season.

funFact: Harpoon clubtail larvae are fierce underwater predators that can shoot out their lower jaw like a spring-loaded harpoon to snatch prey - they can extend this 'labium' up to one-third of their body length in a lightning-fast strike that takes less than 25 milliseconds!
confusionNotes: Harpoon clubtails can be confused with other clubtails in the Phanogomphus genus, but the key is looking at the specific shape and markings of that clubbed tail segment. Memory trick: think 'harpoon point' - the harpoon clubtail's appendages are more pointed and prominent than its clubtail cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Phanogomphus was recently split off from the larger Gomphus genus based on genetic studies, so you might see older field guides listing this species as 'Gomphus descriptus.' This is part of ongoing scientific work to better understand dragonfly relationships - the insects themselves haven't changed, just our understanding of how they're related!
compareHints: Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the harpoon clubtail is distinguished by its specific tail appendage shape and the pattern of yellow markings on its thorax. The lancet clubtail has a more blade-like appearance to its 'club,' while the beaverpond clubtail is typically found in still waters rather than flowing streams. Rapids clubtails prefer faster-moving water and have different thoracic stripes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the lancet clubtail is distinguished by its bright green thorax stripes and green triangular abdominal markings.

Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the Beaverpond Clubtail is most reliably identified by habitat - it strongly prefers beaver ponds and similar still waters over the flowing streams favored by Rapids and Lancet Clubtails.
Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the dusky clubtail lives up to its name with more subdued coloration than the bright yellow Rapids Clubtail or the pale Ashy Clubtail.

Among its Phanogomphus cousins, the Ashy Clubtail is distinguished by its pale coloration — the Dusky Clubtail is much darker, the Rapids Clubtail has more distinct yellow markings, and the Lancet Clubtail is smaller and more delicately built.
